cards.front: What is an accelerator, in the packaging-for-reuse sense this course uses?
cards.back: A working solution packaged so the next engagement configures it rather than rebuilding it: the customer-specific parts are exposed as documented parameters with defaults, the assumptions are written down, and an eval is bundled to prove the asset still works in a new context.
cards.extra: M5 · Packaging for Reuse · Packaging a working build so the next engagement starts from an asset

cards.cloze_text: Most reusable work in an accelerator falls into one of three asset types: {{c1::an Agent Template}}, {{c2::an MCP Server Package}}, and {{c3::an Eval Suite}}.
cards.extra: M5 · Packaging for Reuse · Packaging a working build so the next engagement starts from an asset

cards.front: For an Agent Template accelerator, what does correct packaging require, beyond just having a working system prompt, tool schemas, and loop structure?
cards.back: Pull the domain-specific values into configuration with documented defaults, so a new team sets the values rather than editing the loop.
cards.extra: M5 · Packaging for Reuse · Packaging a working build so the next engagement starts from an asset

cards.front: For an MCP Server Package accelerator, what does correct packaging require?
cards.back: Document each tool's inputs, and let the installing team set the scope, so the server installs into a new environment without code edits.
cards.extra: M5 · Packaging for Reuse · Packaging a working build so the next engagement starts from an asset

cards.front: For an Eval Suite accelerator, what two things must ship together, and why?
cards.back: The graded dataset and the judge rubric, shipped together, so a new team can run them in their own context and confirm the asset still works there.
cards.extra: M5 · Packaging for Reuse · Packaging a working build so the next engagement starts from an asset

cards.front: Why is shipping an agent as a set of loose scripts, instead of a template, a common packaging mistake, even though the scripts run correctly?
cards.back: Every customer-specific value ends up buried in a different file with nothing to configure centrally, so the next team copies and diverges the scripts instead of configuring one documented, reusable asset.
cards.extra: M5 · Packaging for Reuse · Packaging a working build so the next engagement starts from an asset

cards.cloze_text: An accelerator's documentation must cover four things code alone doesn't show: {{c1::the assumptions it makes about its environment}}, {{c2::the inputs it expects}}, {{c3::the failure modes it already handles}}, and {{c4::the eval that defines whether it still works}}.
cards.extra: M5 · Packaging for Reuse · Packaging a working build so the next engagement starts from an asset

cards.front: Why must an accelerator bundle its audit log as part of the package, rather than treating it as optional?
cards.back: A regulated customer's reviewer asks what data the asset touches, what identity it acts under, and what log it leaves — an accelerator without this passes a demo but stalls at the first security review.
cards.extra: M5 · Packaging for Reuse · Packaging a working build so the next engagement starts from an asset

cards.front: When is packaging overhead for an accelerator not worth paying?
cards.back: For a one-off build a customer will never reuse — ship it and move on, without packaging it as an accelerator.
cards.extra: M5 · Packaging for Reuse · Packaging a working build so the next engagement starts from an asset

cards.front: A team's agent template ran successfully and shipped on a deadline, but months later a second team couldn't reuse it and had to rewrite it from scratch. What was the root cause?
cards.back: The build was treated as finished the moment it ran, rather than at the moment it could be reused — customer-specific values (the repo path, model name, review thresholds, prompt fragments) were hardcoded into the loop with no documentation of what was customer-specific, so the second team had nothing to configure and no bundled eval to confirm a guessed fix still worked.
cards.extra: M5 · Packaging for Reuse · The template that shipped fast and could not be reused

cards.cloze_text: A template that runs has not been packaged for reuse. The three warning signs are the absence of: {{c1::parameters where customer-specific values belong}}, {{c2::documentation describing the assumptions}}, and {{c3::a bundled eval proving the asset still works in a different context}}.
cards.extra: M5 · Packaging for Reuse · The template that shipped fast and could not be reused

cards.front: Why should you package a build for reuse while it's still fresh, rather than waiting until a second team actually needs to reuse it?
cards.back: The knowledge of what is customer-specific is most expensive to reconstruct after the people who had it have moved on. Hardcoding is a reasonable shortcut under a deadline, but a working template gives no visible signal that it can't be reused, so the cost stays invisible until someone pays for the rebuild.
cards.extra: M5 · Packaging for Reuse · The template that shipped fast and could not be reused

cards.front: An agent-building function hardcodes the customer's repository path directly inside itself (with a comment marking it as the customer's repo), instead of taking it as a parameter. What's the fix, and what does it let the next team do differently?
cards.back: Add repo_path as a parameter to the function that builds the Agent, and pass it through instead of the hardcoded string. This lets the next team configure the path for their own engagement instead of editing the function's code.
cards.extra: M5 · Packaging for Reuse · Checkpoint 1: Fix the broken accelerator template

cards.front: How does packaging an asset for your own team's reuse (parameters, documented assumptions, a bundled eval) also prepare it for external contribution to a maintainer?
cards.back: The parameters show the asset can be configured rather than rewritten, the documented assumptions tell a maintainer what environment the asset expects, and the bundled eval gives them a way to confirm it still works — an asset packaged for internal reuse is already close to what a maintainer needs to accept it.
cards.extra: M5 · Contributing Back · Moving an asset from private reuse into shared infrastructure a maintainer accepts

cards.cloze_text: The {{c1::Claude Cookbook}} is a GitHub repository of focused reference implementations, designed for self-contained single- or multi-pattern implementations demonstrated clearly and working end to end.
cards.extra: M5 · Contributing Back · Moving an asset from private reuse into shared infrastructure a maintainer accepts

cards.front: Why does sending a full multi-component application to the Claude Cookbook fail to get reviewed, even when the application works well?
cards.back: The Cookbook is built to review one focused pattern, not an entire application — a submission that large doesn't fit what reviewers are looking for and stalls. Putting a full application where a focused example belongs is one of the most common reasons a contribution never gets reviewed.
cards.extra: M5 · Contributing Back · Moving an asset from private reuse into shared infrastructure a maintainer accepts

cards.cloze_text: A maintainer accepts a contribution they can verify. Four things make that possible: {{c1::the code does one thing}}, {{c2::an example shows it running}}, {{c3::a test proves it works}}, and {{c4::a short statement names the assumptions}}.
cards.extra: M5 · Contributing Back · Moving an asset from private reuse into shared infrastructure a maintainer accepts

cards.front: Why must licensing and attribution be confirmed before a contribution goes through technical review, rather than after?
cards.back: Licensing and attribution decide whether a contribution can be accepted at all — code carried in from a customer engagement may have constraints on where it can go, so confirming the right to contribute it (and attributing anything built on) is a gate that must be passed first. Skipping this turns the contribution into a problem the legal team must unwind later.
cards.extra: M5 · Contributing Back · Moving an asset from private reuse into shared infrastructure a maintainer accepts

cards.front: In the contribute-back motion, what part is specifically the Developer's job to prepare, versus what the broader team provides?
cards.back: The Developer's job is technical readiness: the focused code, the example, the test, the statement of assumptions, and the rights check. The engagement context comes from the broader team.
cards.extra: M5 · Contributing Back · Moving an asset from private reuse into shared infrastructure a maintainer accepts

cards.front: A developer's pull request sat open for three weeks with no review, even though the code worked and the developer used it daily. Why did it stall?
cards.back: The maintainer couldn't verify it — there was no test to run, no example proving the behavior, and no statement of what it assumed about the environment. A contribution a reviewer can't verify sits at the back of the queue until someone has time to reconstruct what it does.
cards.extra: M5 · Contributing Back · The pull request a maintainer could not verify

cards.front: Why is it easy for a contribution's author to overlook the need for an example, a test, and an assumptions statement before opening a pull request?
cards.back: The missing context already seems obvious to the person who wrote the code — how it works, what it assumes, that it behaves correctly. To the maintainer none of it is obvious, and a reviewer who must reconstruct intent will always do that reconstruction last, after everything else in the queue.
cards.extra: M5 · Contributing Back · The pull request a maintainer could not verify

cards.front: A developer wants to contribute a focused tool that wraps a single API into a clean function — the snippet is just that function and nothing else. Which channel should it go through, and what readiness item is the snippet currently missing?
cards.back: It goes through the tool's own repository — a focused tool is reviewed there, not in the Cookbook. It's missing a test that proves the wrapper behaves; the function alone isn't enough for a maintainer to verify.
cards.extra: M5 · Contributing Back · Checkpoint 2: Choose the contribution channel and the readiness fix

cards.front: A developer wants to share a full customer-service application whole — including its UI and deployment scripts — as a contribution. Why doesn't it fit the Cookbook as-is, and what has to happen before any part of it can go there?
cards.back: The Cookbook's review is built for one focused pattern, not an entire application, so sending it whole stalls regardless of code quality. The reusable pattern inside it must first be extracted into a focused, self-contained example — only that stripped-down example goes to the Cookbook.
cards.extra: M5 · Contributing Back · Checkpoint 2: Choose the contribution channel and the readiness fix

cards.front: A developer wants to contribute a one-line fix to an existing Cookbook example, carried in from a customer engagement. Which channel does it go through, and what readiness item must be cleared first, even for such a small change?
cards.back: It goes to that existing example's own repository — a fix belongs where the example already lives. The rights check must be cleared first: engagement code can carry a licensing constraint that blocks the merge before any technical review, no matter how small the change.
cards.extra: M5 · Contributing Back · Checkpoint 2: Choose the contribution channel and the readiness fix

cards.front: What makes a statement a valid functional requirement, as opposed to a vague business goal?
cards.back: It names what the system must do, stated with enough detail to check. A vague goal cannot be designed against or verified, while a specific, checkable statement of behavior becomes a line in an eval and a criterion at review.
cards.extra: M5 · Requirements & Lifecycle · From business requirements to functional and infrastructure requirements

cards.cloze_text: Infrastructure requirements are the non-functional constraints a deployment must satisfy. You derive them by asking: {{c1::Latency}} — how fast must a response be, measured where the user is? {{c2::Scale}} — how many requests, at what peak? {{c3::Residency}} — where must data be processed, under which regulation? {{c4::Identity}} — who acts, under what credentials, and what must be auditable?
cards.extra: M5 · Requirements & Lifecycle · From business requirements to functional and infrastructure requirements

cards.front: Why should functional and infrastructure requirements be written down in a short requirements record before a deployment platform is chosen?
cards.back: Because the deployment decision will be reviewed by people who did not gather the requirements. A record covering the functional behaviors, the infrastructure constraints, and which regulation each constraint comes from lets you defend a platform choice as following from the requirements, rather than from familiarity.
cards.extra: M5 · Requirements & Lifecycle · From business requirements to functional and infrastructure requirements

cards.front: When is a full, documented requirements record overkill, with lightweight notes being enough instead?
cards.back: For a throwaway prototype that has no review and touches no regulated data — lightweight notes are enough there.
cards.extra: M5 · Requirements & Lifecycle · From business requirements to functional and infrastructure requirements

cards.front: A regulated EU bank wants an agent that summarizes customer call transcripts for its support team, with summaries reviewed before being stored in the EU. State a valid functional requirement for this system, and explain what makes it checkable rather than just a vague goal.
cards.back: A valid functional requirement: the agent produces a summary that a human approves before it is stored. It's checkable because it's tied to a specific, verifiable business process (human-in-the-loop review) — unlike a vague goal such as 'the agent should be fast and accurate,' which can't be checked, and unlike a cloud-provider or data-location rule, which would be an infrastructure requirement, not a functional one.
cards.extra: M5 · Requirements & Lifecycle · Checkpoint 3: extract the requirements

cards.front: A regulated EU bank wants an agent that summarizes customer call transcripts for its support team, with summaries reviewed before being stored in the EU. State a valid infrastructure requirement for this system, and explain why it counts as infrastructure rather than functional or a mere design choice.
cards.back: A valid infrastructure requirement: transcript data is processed in the EU. It's checkable and tied to a specific regulatory constraint (data residency) — unlike 'summarizes using a pre-approved prompt template' (a design choice, not an infrastructure requirement) or 'a human reviews each summary before it's stored' (a functional requirement, not an infrastructure one).
cards.extra: M5 · Requirements & Lifecycle · Checkpoint 3: extract the requirements

cards.cloze_text: A Claude application moves through seven lifecycle phases: {{c1::Requirements}} (capture functional and infrastructure needs), {{c2::Design}} (choose the platform, model, and trust boundaries), {{c3::Build}} (write the agent, tools, and prompts), {{c4::Test}} (evals, unit, integration, and end-to-end checks), {{c5::Deploy}} (pin the version, gate promotion on the eval), {{c6::Operate}} (instrument cost, latency, and errors; enforce guardrails), and {{c7::Iterate}} (feed production findings back into requirements).
cards.extra: M5 · Requirements & Lifecycle · Systems lifecycle for Claude applications

cards.front: What is a 'gate' in the systems lifecycle, and what discipline does it enforce?
cards.back: A gate is a decision to move from one lifecycle phase to the next — it's where a regulated engagement keeps control. For example, you don't move from design to build until the platform satisfies the residency requirement, and you don't move from deploy toward full production until the new version clears the eval against the pinned baseline. The discipline is placing engineering work in the right phase and never skipping a gate.
cards.extra: M5 · Requirements & Lifecycle · Systems lifecycle for Claude applications

cards.front: When is it acceptable to collapse the lifecycle phases together instead of gating between them?
cards.back: For a one-off experiment, phases may collapse — but a regulated deployment cannot skip the gates between phases.
cards.extra: M5 · Requirements & Lifecycle · Systems lifecycle for Claude applications

cards.front: Writing an eval suite and its rubric belongs to which lifecycle phase, and gating a new version's promotion to production on that eval's result belongs to which phase? Why are they different phases?
cards.back: Writing the eval suite and rubric is the Test phase. Gating promotion on its result is the Deploy phase. They differ because building the measurement tool (test) is a separate step from using its result to make the go/no-go release decision (deploy).
cards.extra: M5 · Requirements & Lifecycle · Checkpoint 4: place the work in the right phase

cards.front: A team chooses Amazon Bedrock for a project specifically because the customer already holds its compliance posture there. Which lifecycle phase does this platform decision belong to, and why isn't it 'requirements'?
cards.back: Design. The compliance need itself (e.g., data must stay in a specific region under a specific regulation) is the requirement; choosing the specific platform that satisfies that requirement is a design choice made after the requirement is already known.
cards.extra: M5 · Requirements & Lifecycle · Checkpoint 4: place the work in the right phase

cards.front: Instrumenting token cost and latency per call in a live production system belongs to which lifecycle phase, and how does that differ from testing?
cards.back: Operate. Testing verifies behavior before deployment; instrumenting cost and latency happens continuously after deployment, on live production traffic.
cards.extra: M5 · Requirements & Lifecycle · Checkpoint 4: place the work in the right phase

cards.front: What usually determines which deployment platform a Claude workload runs on, more than technical merit alone?
cards.back: The customer's existing cloud infrastructure, identity management, and compliance agreements — the platform decision is usually shaped by which platform the customer already trusts and operates on, not by technical merit alone.
cards.extra: M5 · Deployment & Versioning · Choosing where a Claude workload runs and versioning what ships

cards.front: What's the main practical advantage of the first-party Claude API over the other deployment platforms?
cards.back: It's Anthropic's own environment, and it typically receives new features first.
cards.extra: M5 · Deployment & Versioning · Choosing where a Claude workload runs and versioning what ships

cards.front: How does 'Claude Platform on AWS' differ from Amazon Bedrock in terms of whose model IDs and lifecycle it follows, and where inference runs?
cards.back: Claude Platform on AWS is accessed through the customer's AWS account but uses Anthropic's own model IDs and lifecycle, with inference Anthropic-operated outside the AWS boundary — unlike Bedrock, which uses its own API and versioning and keeps data inside the AWS boundary.
cards.extra: M5 · Deployment & Versioning · Choosing where a Claude workload runs and versioning what ships

cards.front: Amazon Bedrock offers two different integrations for Claude. What API does each one use?
cards.back: Claude in Amazon Bedrock uses the Messages API at /anthropic/v1/messages, with broad feature parity with the first-party API. Claude on Amazon Bedrock (legacy) uses the InvokeModel/Converse APIs with ARN-versioned model identifiers.
cards.extra: M5 · Deployment & Versioning · Choosing where a Claude workload runs and versioning what ships

cards.front: Claude in Microsoft Foundry offers two hosting forms. What are they, and which specific models are 'Hosted on Azure' as of this course?
cards.back: Hosted on Azure (currently Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Haiku 4.5, with inference running end-to-end on Azure infrastructure) and Hosted on Anthropic (all other Foundry Claude models, with inference on Anthropic-operated infrastructure). Residency assumptions for regulated customers depend on which hosting form the specific model uses.
cards.extra: M5 · Deployment & Versioning · Choosing where a Claude workload runs and versioning what ships

cards.front: How do Bedrock and Vertex AI each handle identity and the data boundary?
cards.back: Bedrock uses AWS identity and keeps data inside the customer's AWS boundary. Vertex uses Google Cloud identity and boundary. Both offer regional routing when residency is a constraint.
cards.extra: M5 · Deployment & Versioning · Choosing where a Claude workload runs and versioning what ships

cards.front: Why should you pin a full Claude model ID instead of using a convenience alias like opus or sonnet in a production deployment?
cards.back: Aliases are convenient but evolve over time and may resolve to different versions across deployment platforms — an unpinned deployment makes every upstream model update a silent, untracked change to your output. A pinned full model ID resolves to a fixed snapshot, so an upstream update becomes a deliberate choice instead.
cards.extra: M5 · Deployment & Versioning · Choosing where a Claude workload runs and versioning what ships

cards.front: What's the process for promoting a new pinned model or prompt version to full production?
cards.back: Gate promotion on the eval suite: send the new version to a portion of traffic, compare its score against the pinned baseline, and promote it to full production or roll back based on the result. This is where the eval stops being a one-time test and becomes the deployment gate.
cards.extra: M5 · Deployment & Versioning · Choosing where a Claude workload runs and versioning what ships

cards.front: Besides pinning the model version itself, what else should be versioned, and why keep the prior version available?
cards.back: Version the prompt and the asset alongside the code, and keep the prior version available so a regression can be rolled back rather than hotfixed in place.
cards.extra: M5 · Deployment & Versioning · Choosing where a Claude workload runs and versioning what ships

cards.cloze_text: The six Claude deployment platforms are: {{c1::the first-party Claude API}}, {{c2::Claude Platform on AWS}}, {{c3::Claude in Amazon Bedrock}}, {{c4::Claude on Amazon Bedrock (legacy)}}, {{c5::Google Vertex AI}}, and {{c6::third-party platforms}}.
cards.extra: M5 · Deployment & Versioning · Choosing where a Claude workload runs and versioning what ships

cards.front: A team deployed using the moving alias opus as the model reference instead of a pinned ID. Sometime later, production output parsing broke with no code change on the team's side. What happened, and why couldn't they roll back?
cards.back: The alias silently advanced to a new Opus version, which changed the response's output shape (a KeyError on a field the parser expected). They couldn't roll back because no pinned prior version had been retained — the deployment was never pinned in the first place, so there was no earlier snapshot to fall back to.
cards.extra: M5 · Deployment & Versioning · The deployment that broke when the model alias moved

cards.front: After the incident where a moving model alias broke production parsing, the team shipped a hotfix to the parser. Why did that hotfix not actually fix the underlying problem?
cards.back: The hotfix repaired the immediate symptom (the parser) but left the unpinned deployment in place — the root cause, using a moving alias with no pinned prior version, was untouched, so the same failure mode could recur on the next alias advance.
cards.extra: M5 · Deployment & Versioning · The deployment that broke when the model alias moved

cards.cloze_text: To keep model-alias drift from reaching production: {{c1::pin the full model ID}} instead of a moving alias, so an upstream update is adopted on purpose; {{c2::keep the prior pinned version available}}, so a regression is a rollback rather than a hotfix; and {{c3::gate the new version through your eval before promoting it}}, so an output-shape change surfaces in a test run instead of live.
cards.extra: M5 · Deployment & Versioning · The deployment that broke when the model alias moved

cards.front: A customer runs AWS with a data-residency requirement and needs to be able to roll back a model update. Which deployment platform satisfies this, and why not the first-party API or Google Vertex AI?
cards.back: Amazon Bedrock — it keeps identity and data inside the AWS boundary the customer has already cleared. The first-party API or Vertex AI would each move identity and data outside that already-cleared boundary.
cards.extra: M5 · Deployment & Versioning · Checkpoint 5: Match the deployment platform and version pin to each scenario

cards.front: A customer runs AWS with a data-residency requirement and needs to be able to roll back a model update. Given Amazon Bedrock is the right platform, what identity should the deployment use, and what kind of model reference — an alias or a pinned ID?
cards.back: An AWS identity reference, not an Anthropic API key (which would move identity outside the cleared AWS boundary), and a pinned full model ID with the anthropic. prefix, not a moving alias — the pinned ID makes an upstream model change something the team adopts deliberately, while an alias would drift underneath them.
cards.extra: M5 · Deployment & Versioning · Checkpoint 5: Match the deployment platform and version pin to each scenario

cards.front: A customer runs AWS with a data-residency requirement and needs to be able to roll back a model update. What configuration choice actually enables that rollback, and why is a pinned model ID alone not sufficient for it?
cards.back: Retaining the prior pinned version is what gives you a rollback target. A pinned model ID with no retained prior version still can't roll back — pinning stops silent drift, but only keeping the old version around lets you actually revert to it.
cards.extra: M5 · Deployment & Versioning · Checkpoint 5: Match the deployment platform and version pin to each scenario

cards.front: What does latency depend on when comparing Claude deployment platforms, and why is measuring it from your own laptop misleading?
cards.back: Latency depends on where the platform runs relative to the customer and how access to new features is routed. Measuring from your laptop hides the round-trip penalty that appears once the workload actually runs from where the customer is — the number is only accurate when measured from the customer's actual region against their actual payload.
cards.extra: M5 · Comparing Platforms · Comparing platforms on latency, compliance, and cost so the choice survives review

cards.front: What's the latency/feature trade-off between an in-region cloud platform and the first-party Claude API?
cards.back: A platform running in the customer's own cloud region can reduce round-trip time versus a first-party endpoint located farther away, but the first-party API typically receives new capabilities before other platforms do.
cards.extra: M5 · Comparing Platforms · Comparing platforms on latency, compliance, and cost so the choice survives review

cards.front: Within Amazon Bedrock specifically, what choice acts as the primary residency control, and what else can it affect?
cards.back: The choice between global and regional endpoints — it's the primary residency control within Bedrock, and it can also affect cost. You should measure from the customer's actual region against both options before committing.
cards.extra: M5 · Comparing Platforms · Comparing platforms on latency, compliance, and cost so the choice survives review

cards.front: Why do regulated financial or healthcare customers treat compliance and residency requirements as pass-or-fail rather than as one tradeoff to balance against others?
cards.back: A customer who already holds a certification on one cloud is unlikely to re-certify on another, and available compliance certifications plus who can audit access differ by platform — for a regulated customer, these are gating constraints, not things to weigh against latency or cost.
cards.extra: M5 · Comparing Platforms · Comparing platforms on latency, compliance, and cost so the choice survives review

cards.front: For a customer requiring EU-only data residency, why might the first-party Claude API not be sufficient on its own, and what should you confirm for a third-party platform like Microsoft Foundry?
cards.back: The first-party Claude API may not offer EU data residency (confirm current regional coverage) — EU-only residency typically requires Bedrock or Vertex AI instead. For Foundry, hosting is per-model: Azure-hosted Foundry models run inference end-to-end on Azure infrastructure, but Anthropic-hosted Foundry models do not satisfy EU regional residency requirements, so residency must be confirmed per model and deployment with Microsoft.
cards.extra: M5 · Comparing Platforms · Comparing platforms on latency, compliance, and cost so the choice survives review

cards.front: Per-token rates are broadly aligned across Claude deployment platforms, so what actually drives total cost differences between them?
cards.back: Data egress, platform fees, and integration effort — a lower token price can end up costing more in total once data transfer and integration are factored in, so you should instrument total cost per call for each platform rather than comparing token price alone.
cards.extra: M5 · Comparing Platforms · Comparing platforms on latency, compliance, and cost so the choice survives review

cards.front: When can you skip doing the full latency, compliance, and cost comparison across deployment platforms?
cards.back: When the customer's compliance requirement is already pass-or-fail — that constraint determines the platform placement on its own, without needing to weigh the other dimensions.
cards.extra: M5 · Comparing Platforms · Comparing platforms on latency, compliance, and cost so the choice survives review

cards.cloze_text: {{c1::Data residency}} is a rule that a customer's data must be processed in a specific country or region.
cards.extra: M5 · Comparing Platforms · Comparing platforms on latency, compliance, and cost so the choice survives review

cards.front: A developer chose the deployment platform their team was already familiar with for a regulated customer's project, and the build passed all its functional tests. What went wrong at the customer's security review, and why did familiarity fail to predict it?
cards.back: The reviewer found the selected platform did not satisfy the customer's data-residency requirement — a less-familiar platform would have satisfied it through regional options the customer had already cleared. Familiarity only answered whether the team could build quickly; it never answered whether the deployment would pass the residency review, which was the test that actually determined whether it could ship. The integration had to be rebuilt.
cards.extra: M5 · Comparing Platforms · The platform picked on familiarity that failed residency

cards.front: After a platform choice failed a customer's residency review late, at the go/no-go stage, what's the fix for avoiding this failure on future regulated engagements?
cards.back: Identify residency and compliance constraints early, during scoping, and let them influence the platform choice before familiarity does — for a regulated customer these constraints are often pass-or-fail. Checking early costs a scoping conversation; checking late costs an entire rebuild.
cards.extra: M5 · Comparing Platforms · The platform picked on familiarity that failed residency

cards.front: A team measured deployment latency from their dev laptop (180ms — looked fine) and selected a platform based on team familiarity. The customer is in eu-west and requires EU-only data residency. The deployment was rejected with the reason 'data processed outside EU.' What's the actual fix, and why won't optimizing the parser or adding a caching layer solve it?
cards.back: Remeasure latency from the customer's actual region (eu-west) and select the platform whose region satisfies EU-only residency. The rejection reason names data residency, not speed or cost, so optimizing the parser's latency or adding a caching layer both treat a dimension that was never the problem.
cards.extra: M5 · Comparing Platforms · Checkpoint 6: Diagnose the platform mismatch from a comparison trace

cards.front: What makes connecting multiple Claude-capability components into one workflow risky, even when each component works correctly on its own?
cards.back: Every connection between components creates a place where identity, secrets, and untrusted input can cross. Each component contributes a capability the others don't have, but the connections themselves are where risk concentrates — so you map which component does what before connecting anything.
cards.extra: M5 · Trust Boundaries · Coordinating several Claude deployments with the trust boundaries holding under review

cards.cloze_text: The {{c1::trust boundary}} is the point where data or instructions move from one deployment environment to another; content fetched by one component must be treated as {{c2::data}}, not instructions, once it reaches the next component.
cards.extra: M5 · Trust Boundaries · Coordinating several Claude deployments with the trust boundaries holding under review

cards.front: Why can't you assume a component is trustworthy at its boundary just because it worked correctly on its own?
cards.back: Working correctly in isolation says nothing about the seam where it hands data to the next component. The core discipline is to identify every seam as a boundary, rather than assuming trust carries over from a component that behaved well by itself.
cards.extra: M5 · Trust Boundaries · Coordinating several Claude deployments with the trust boundaries holding under review

cards.front: In a multi-component application, what determines how contained the application is as a whole?
cards.back: The application is only as contained as its most privileged seam — a single component scoped too broadly becomes the weak point even when every other component is properly scoped. Each component must be scoped to the least privilege its specific role in the workflow requires.
cards.extra: M5 · Trust Boundaries · Coordinating several Claude deployments with the trust boundaries holding under review

cards.front: What must a regulated review of a multi-component Claude application justify across the whole application?
cards.back: Audit logging, data-residency decisions, and permission controls across the full application. For regulated deployments, Bedrock and Vertex AI are typically the platforms that satisfy regional residency constraints, and ZDR and HIPAA BAA eligibility need confirming per component.
cards.extra: M5 · Trust Boundaries · Coordinating several Claude deployments with the trust boundaries holding under review

cards.front: In a multi-component app made of a first-party API entry point, a Claude Code task, and an MCP server, what's the trust boundary at the API's seam, and what control enforces it?
cards.back: The boundary is the request entering the app from outside. The control is input validation plus the identity the call runs under.
cards.extra: M5 · Trust Boundaries · Coordinating several Claude deployments with the trust boundaries holding under review

cards.front: In that same multi-component app (API, Claude Code task, MCP server), what's the trust boundary at the MCP server's seam, and what control enforces it?
cards.back: The boundary is the system access the server holds on the app's behalf, such as reaching a customer system. The control is scoping the server to least privilege and logging the access.
cards.extra: M5 · Trust Boundaries · Coordinating several Claude deployments with the trust boundaries holding under review

cards.front: Two developers wired together three components that each had passed their own tests. What critical seam did they overlook, and why did it matter?
cards.back: The seam where the Claude Code task's fetched content flowed straight into the next call's prompt. Each component was trusted in isolation, but the seam between them was not — content fetched from a customer page is untrusted, and if it carries instructions, the next component runs them, because that seam was never marked as a boundary.
cards.extra: M5 · Trust Boundaries · The seam nobody marked as a boundary

cards.front: In a multi-component app, does a trust boundary exist only once someone explicitly marks it and adds a control there, or does it exist wherever data crosses environments regardless of whether it's marked?
cards.back: It exists wherever data or instructions cross from one deployment environment to another, regardless of whether anyone marks it. In the unmarked-seam failure, the boundary existed in the data flow between the Claude Code task and the next call — it just wasn't marked, so no control checked it. Marking it is what makes a control possible; leaving it unmarked doesn't make the risk go away.
cards.extra: M5 · Trust Boundaries · The seam nobody marked as a boundary

cards.front: In a wired multi-component app where a Claude Code task fetches a customer page and the result is about to be passed into the next call, what should wrap that fetched content first, and why?
cards.back: Wrap it so the next component treats it as data, not as instructions (e.g., a treat_as_data(...) wrapper). This closes the injection seam where untrusted fetched content could otherwise be run as if it were trusted instructions.
cards.extra: M5 · Trust Boundaries · Checkpoint 7: Complete the multi-component boundary configuration

cards.front: In a multi-component app, an MCP server is the most privileged component because it reaches the customer's database directly. What identity scope should it be given, and why does over-scoping it matter more than over-scoping the other components?
cards.back: Least-privilege, read-only scope, so a steered action can't reach beyond its intended task. It matters more here because the application is only as contained as its most privileged seam — an over-broad scope on the MCP server becomes the weak point for the whole app, even if every other component is properly scoped.

cards.cloze_text: Auditing a packaged accelerator deployed to production means checking three distinct layers for defects: {{c1::packaging (are customer-specific values parameterized, not hardcoded?)}}, {{c2::deployment and versioning (is the model pinned to a full ID with a retained prior version, not a moving alias?)}}, and {{c3::the multi-component trust boundary (is fetched content treated as data, not passed through as instructions?)}}.
cards.extra: M5 · Cumulative Task · Cumulative task: Find all three, explain each, write the correction

cards.front: In a corrected accelerator deployment — parameterized repo path, pinned Bedrock model ID, a retained rollback version, and fetched content wrapped as data — what final assertion should still run before the new version is promoted, and what does it check?
cards.back: An assertion that runs the bundled eval suite against the new pinned model and requires its score to be greater than or equal to the pinned baseline score before the version ships. Even a deployment that's already fixed on packaging, pinning, and boundaries still needs this eval gate before promotion.

cards.cloze_text: {{c1::Contribution readiness}} is what a maintainer needs to verify a contribution: focused code, a runnable example, a test that proves the behavior, a statement of environment assumptions, and confirmed rights to contribute the code.
